newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. envoy fails to get Zaire to back safe havens.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy fails to get Zaire to back safe havens.

text.p: A U.N. envoy apparently failed to persuade Zairean authorities during talks on Saturday to agree to safe havens inside Zaire for over a million war refugees.
Zaire maintained after talks with envoy Raymond Chretien that any international relief operation for the Rwandan and Burundian refugees must be mounted in their own countries.
The refugees fled violence in their homeland and are still afraid to go home. Scattered from camps by war in eastern Zaire, they are dying in thousands in the jungle, aid workers say.

"The government took a firm decision yesterday that food destined for the refugees should be distributed in Rwanda to facilitate the return of the refugees to their country of origin," Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told reporters.
But Kengo, a part-Tutsi accused at home of not dealing firmly with an ethnic-Tutsi rebellion in eastern Zaire, said the government welcomed U.N. proposals for an intervention force.
Early on Saturday the Security Council called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force for the troubled region but put off its deployment until a later stage.
The interim resolution, adopted unanimously, asked states involved to report back as soon as possible to enable the Council to give final approval.

"The U.N. special envoy has just informed us of the decision taken by the U.N. Security Council. The resolution talks of the military support necessary to achieve humanitarian objectives. We are agreed with this," Kengo said.
Zaire made it clear as Chretien arrived on Friday night that it believes an intervention force should facilitate the return home of the refugees who have lived on its soil for up to three years.

But aid workers and several international politicians are advocating swift intervention to get aid to refugees because of what they term a humanitarian tragedy unfolding in the jungles of eastern Zaire where refugees are dying of thirst, hunger and disease.
"I think I now have a much better perception of the attitude of the positions of Rwandan and Zairean authorities," said Chretien, who arrived in Zaire from talks in Rwanda.
"I intend over the next few days to remain in contact with the Rwandan and Zairean authorities to advance first and foremost the question of security," he told reporters.
"The humanitarian operation will only be possible when there is security on the ground," he added.

France and Spain have offered troops for the force. But, Rwanda's Tutsi government is mistrustful of France as an ally of the Hutu regime ousted after genocidal massacres in 1994. It says a French military intervention in 1994 facilitated the escape of genocide leaders.
Some of the refugees include armed former Hutu soldiers, a source of hostility between Rwanda and their Zairean hosts.
Zaire in turn accuses Rwanda's Tutsi-led army of fighting alongside the Banyamulenge Tuitsi rebels who have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces since fighting erupted on October 18.

Asked if Zaire saw foreign military intervention as a chance to reclaim territory, Kengo said: "The (U.N.) resolution speaks of the inviolability of frontiers and the integrity of territory. How can we understand otherwise?"
